globalExpectedConditions: Pressure p is absolute gas pressure, not excess pressure above atmosphere. Gauge indication alone cannot be substituted into the gas law.
Boyle-Mariotte comparisons use the same fixed amount/composition of gas, without leakage or a phase change that removes gas from the sample.

The compared states have the same temperature. During an isothermal compression or expansion, adequate thermal contact and sufficiently slow change can compensate compression/expansion energy; an ordinary rapid pump stroke does not establish isothermal behavior.
A thermodynamic state is described by p, V and t; a process connects states. Change of thermodynamic state is not synonymous with a solid/liquid/gas phase change.
p and V are positive, consistently measured quantities. The source ratios and products are preserved exactly, including equation references 2-1 and 2-2.

The law is exact for an ideal-gas model at fixed amount and temperature, and approximate for real gases sufficiently dilute and away from condensation. No universal accuracy, arbitrary temperature range or numerical threshold is inferred.
Different-temperature isotherms of the same gas amount are compared at the same volume. A hotter isotherm is above a colder one; movement between these curves is not itself an isothermal process.
All unregistered source mathematical and number tokens must remain. Historical or pedagogical qualifications are prose, not invented numerical or formula errata.
The source's Boyle 1660 date must be explicitly attributed to the source textbook. This review does not independently verify history, replace the date, or invent an erratum.
Mercury apparatus is historical description only. Preserve the toxicity/spill warning and prohibit child replication; do not turn the historical sequence into construction or operating instructions.

Instrument letters M, B and L are source labels, not numerical data. A ruler provides length; volume determination requires apparatus geometry/calibration. No scale units, calibration constants, gauge type, range or readings are inferred.
Figure and caption identities are reviewed as text metadata only. No unseen fig17, fig18 or fig19 scientific/visual approval is granted.

blocks.expectedMeaning: Pressure, volume and temperature are related state parameters for a gas. Holding the gas amount fixed, changing one can require at least one other to change. A parameter relation can be used to determine temperature, as referenced in section 11.
conditions: Fixed gas amount and specified constraints; do not imply that both other parameters must always change.
State description is distinct from the process and from phase change.
blocks.uncertainty: The source introductory generalization must not be read as an unconstrained or universal causal rule.

blocks.expectedMeaning: An experimentally simpler process holds one of p, V or t constant and studies the quantitative relationship between the other two.
conditions: Same fixed amount of gas.
A process with one constant parameter is not a new static state or a phase-transition definition.
blocks.uncertainty: This is a pedagogical route to gas laws, not a claim that simultaneous parameter changes make relations impossible.

blocks.expectedMeaning: The source attributes the first gas law to British scholar Boyle in 1660 and names his work about the spring of air. Compressed air in a bicycle pump gives a familiar qualitative spring-like resistance analogy.
conditions: The analogy is not Hooke's law or proof of an isothermal pV law.
A pump can heat the air; analogy and quantitative law must remain separate.
blocks.historicalAttribution: 1660 is explicitly a SOURCE-ATTRIBUTED historical claim, not independently endorsed chronology. Preserve the source work-title attribution without replacing the date.
blocks.uncertainty: No external history verification is authorized or performed.

blocks.expectedMeaning: Boyle studied pressure-volume change at constant temperature. An isothermal process keeps the gas temperature unchanged. A constant-temperature surrounding system can serve as a thermal reservoir; sufficiently stable atmosphere can play this role.
conditions: Fixed amount of gas.
Thermal contact must be effective and change sufficiently slow for approximate constant gas temperature.
Do not endorse the source's 'only' as a universal definition or say stable air temperature alone guarantees stable gas temperature.
blocks.uncertainty: No numerical rate of compression or temperature tolerance is supplied by the source.

blocks.expectedMeaning: Historical bent-tube mercury experiment confines a fixed air sample. Equal liquid levels initially imply gas pressure equal to atmospheric pressure. The source reports a 760 mm height difference, a pressure increase of one original pressure amount (doubling), and halving of air volume, motivating inverse pressure-volume dependence.
conditions: Constant temperature and fixed gas amount.
Absolute pressure includes atmospheric pressure plus the hydrostatic excess; do not confuse the 760 mm difference with total gas pressure.
Attribute the source's numerical doubling account to its atmospheric-pressure convention rather than universal local weather pressure.
Narrative must be past-tense description, not an instruction to add mercury or build equipment.
blocks.historicalAttribution: The 760 mm and doubling observation is the source's historical experimental account; no alternative numbers or conversions are authorized.
blocks.uncertainty: No exact local atmospheric-pressure value, thermometer reading, timing or observed instrument scale is independently known.

blocks.expectedMeaning: The source attributes an independent later conclusion to French physicist Mariotte. For the same gas amount at constant temperature, pressure varies inversely with volume; state labels pair V1 with p1 and V2 with p2, yielding p2/p1 = V1/V2.
conditions: Absolute pressures, not gauge pressures.
Fixed gas amount; same temperature.
Ideal-gas model or stated real-gas approximation.
blocks.historicalAttribution: Preserve Mariotte's independent-result attribution; do not add an unverified discovery date.
blocks.uncertainty: None in the ratio's mathematics under the stated conditions.

blocks.expectedMeaning: The inverse ratio gives equal pressure-volume products for two states of the same gas amount at constant temperature, or pV constant when t is constant.

blocks.uncertainty: The source's t notation stays t; no temperature ratios or Celsius proportionality are implied.
